title: Artabhaga: "when a man dies, what does not leave him?" — karma (3.2)
hook: asked what's left of a person after death, Yajnavalkya takes his questioner's hand and walks him out of the room
tomorrow: Bhujyu asks where the Parikshitas went

segments.voice: Yesterday, atimukti: Ashvala asked how ritual frees anyone from death, and each priest turned out to be a part of the person. Your line was the priest who goes beyond.

The second challenger is Artabhaga, and his last question is one people still ask. When a person dies, he says, their speech goes into fire, their breath into the wind, their eye into the sun, their mind into the moon, their body into the earth, their hair into the plants and trees, their blood into the waters. Then where is that person? And this time, Yajnavalkya won't answer in front of the crowd. Artabhaga, my friend, he says. Take my hand. This is for the two of us alone.
screen: `EVERYTHING GOES BACK.` → `THEN WHERE IS THAT PERSON?` → `TAKE MY HAND.`

segments.voice: Artabhaga's questions start dry. How many graspers are there, and how many over-graspers? Eight, Yajnavalkya says. The tongue grasps, and taste grasps it back. The eye grasps, and form grabs the eye. The ear and sound, the mind and desire, the hands and work. Everything we take hold of takes hold of us. Then closer to the bone. When a person dies, do the breaths leave them? No, they gather inside; the body swells and lies still. When a person dies, what does not leave them? The name, Yajnavalkya says. The name is endless. All of that in public. Then the last question, where is the person when everything has gone back, and the hand, and the walk out of the room. The text tells us only this about their private talk. What they talked about was karma. What they praised was karma. A person becomes good by good action, and bad by bad action. And Artabhaga fell silent. Karma means action, the thing you do, and it had been a word of the ritual: the rite performed correctly. Here, two people step outside and talk about it as the thread of a person's life, carried past death. Some readers hear in it an early statement of the idea in the Upanishads. Why whisper it? The text doesn't say. Some think the teaching was new; some think it was simply too serious for a contest. Either way, a crowd waited outside while two men held hands and talked about what we do.
screen: `EVERYTHING WE GRASP GRASPS US.` · `WHAT DOES NOT LEAVE? THE NAME.` · `WHAT THEY PRAISED WAS KARMA.` · `GOOD BY GOOD ACTION, BAD BY BAD.` · then, large: `THE NAME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has died, someone you knew or someone you've only heard of, and say their name silently. Notice that it still brings a face, a voice, a way of doing things. Then let one thing they did come to mind, good or ordinary, and hold the name and the action together.
Artabhaga. The questioner Yajnavalkya took aside, and the word the two of them praised in private: karma, action, the thing you do.
Your line: the name. Tomorrow, a challenger brings a question he heard from a spirit. That's day three hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Hindus remember the dead by name in shraddha rites, offering food and water to ancestors named in a family line; teachers of the Upanishads point to Artabhaga's dialogue as an early statement of karma.

original.note: Sanskrit karma (stem karman), from kṛ, to do: action, deed, and in the Vedas the ritual act.

what a scholar hears: in 3.2.13 karma becomes moral cause (good by good action, bad by bad), and it is said in private; some readers hear an early statement of the idea here.
